- If sentiment history shows recent negative signals (e.g., -1.00 or 0.00), reduce forecasted price peaks and avoid over-optimistic spikes.  
- When sentiment is consistently positive (e.g., 1.00 across recent days), model should not over-forecast downward trends — expect mean reversion toward prior range.  
- If model forecasts a sharp upward spike followed by a steep decline, reduce the magnitude of the spike and add a downward correction lag (e.g., 2–3 days).  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the model consistently overestimates early days (e.g., first 5–7 days) and underestimates later days, apply a “late-cycle discount” — reduce forecasted values after day 15–20.  
- If sentiment history includes multiple 0.00 or negative values, model should not assume continuation of bullish momentum — expect price to revert to 1–2 standard deviations below recent highs.  
- Avoid forecasting price above 10% above the 18-day moving average unless sentiment is strongly bullish (e.g., 1.00 for 3+ consecutive days).  
- If sentiment turns negative after a peak, model should reduce forecasted price by 5–10% for the next 3–5 days, even if model shows no immediate drop.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the model’s first 5–7 days are significantly above true outcome, apply a “forecast decay” rule — reduce forecasted values by 1–2% per day after day 5.
